claims.text: Tungsten is a candidate material for high-temperature, high-heat-flux fusion reactor components.
Formation of short-range ordered precipitates in tungsten reduces phonon scattering times.
Reduced phonon scattering times caused by SRO precipitates decrease tungsten's lattice thermal conductivity.
Controlling SRO precipitate density can tailor lattice heat transport in tungsten.
High-purity tungsten can have a negligible initial population of SRO precipitates.
Controlled thermal or chemical processing can introduce controlled quantities of SRO precipitates into tungsten.
Fusion plasma-facing components operate under severe particle and heat fluxes and elevated temperatures.
The relevant operating-temperature range extends from several hundred degrees Celsius to about 1000 degrees Celsius.
The SRO precipitates are nanometer-scale and dispersed within the tungsten matrix.
SRO precipitates act as phonon-scattering centers in tungsten.
Increasing SRO precipitate density will produce a measurable decrease in lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine tungsten.
Pure tungsten with negligible SRO precipitates has intrinsically high lattice thermal conductivity.
There is a temperature and processing regime in which lattice conduction dominates tungsten's heat transport.
Electron scattering or radiation damage can overwhelm the thermal-transport effect attributed to SRO precipitates.
Direct experimental data on phonon-precipitate interactions in tungsten are limited.
